name: Battle of Cannae
info: Hannibal's Carthaginian army surrounded and destroyed most of a larger Roman and allied army under the consuls Paullus and Varro at Cannae in Apulia in 216 BCE, during the Second Punic War.

facts.date: 2 August 216 BCE according to Macrobius, citing the annalist Quadrigarius; P. S. Derow identified the Julian equivalent as 1 July 216 BCE, and others have suggested other dates
facts.place: Near the ancient village of Cannae on the left bank of the river Aufidus in Apulia, south-east Italy
facts.sides: Rome and its Italian allies under the consuls Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Gaius Terentius Varro, with approximately 86,000 men by a general estimate; Carthage and its allies under Hannibal, perhaps 40,000 to 50,000, a figure to be treated with caution
facts.outcome: Most of the Roman army was surrounded and killed; ancient and modern figures for the dead range widely. Capua and several other Italian cities went over to Hannibal, but Rome refused to make peace.

t: Ancient and modern figures for Roman dead range from 10,500 to 16,000 (Cantalupi) to 70,000 (Polybius), and figures for ancient battles, Carthaginian ones above all, are often unreliable.
Hannibal's centre gave ground step by step while his African infantry and cavalry closed round the Romans, who were packed so tightly that they could hardly use their weapons.
Rome did not accept Hannibal's offer to ransom prisoners or to make peace, raised new legions and fought on for 14 more years until the Battle of Zama.
dyk: Within three campaign seasons, about 20 months, Rome is said to have lost one fifth, some 150,000, of its male citizens over 17, and it buried people alive as a sacrifice after the defeat.
ev: Hannibal crosses the Pyrenees and Alps into Italy and defeats the Romans at the Trebia
Hannibal defeats the Romans at Lake Trasimene, and Quintus Fabius Maximus is made dictator and avoids pitched battle
Varro and Paullus are elected consuls and given a newly raised army of unprecedented size
Hannibal seizes the supply depot at Cannae and the consuls march south to meet him
Hannibal's army encircles and destroys most of the Roman army at Cannae
Capua and other Italian cities defect to Hannibal; Rome rejects his offer to ransom prisoners
Hannibal first attacks Rome, five years after Cannae
The Romans defeat Hannibal at Zama, ending the war

sections.background:
Hannibal crossed the Pyrenees and Alps in the summer and early autumn of 218 BCE and won major victories at the Trebia and at Lake Trasimene. The Romans then appointed Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus dictator. Fabius used attrition warfare, cutting Hannibal's supply lines and avoiding pitched battle, which grew unpopular as the Romans recovered from the shock. Most wanted a quick end to the war, and it was feared that if Hannibal went on plundering Italy unopposed, Rome's allies might defect for their own safety.

The Senate did not renew Fabius's powers, and command passed to the consuls Gnaeus Servilius Geminus and Marcus Atilius Regulus. In 216 BCE Gaius Terentius Varro and Lucius Aemilius Paullus were elected consuls, given a newly raised army of unprecedented size and told to engage Hannibal. Polybius writes that most wars were decided by one consul and two legions with their allies, but that in the alarm of that year Rome resolved to bring in eight legions, each of 5,000 men besides allies.

Ordinarily each consul commanded his own part of the army, but since the armies were combined, Roman law required the consuls to alternate command daily. In the spring of 216 BCE Hannibal seized the large supply depot at Cannae in the Apulian plain, placing himself between the Romans and a crucial source of supply. The consuls marched south and after two days found him on the left bank of the Aufidus, and camped 8 kilometres away.
sections.forces:
Estimates of the Roman strength vary. Rome normally used four legions of 4,000 foot and 200 horse; for the first time, according to contemporary Roman sources, eight legions of 5,000 foot and 300 horse were fielded, with allies of the same infantry strength and 900 horse for each legion. The eight legions form a core of some 40,000 men and an estimated 2,400 cavalry, and a general estimate is about 86,000 Roman and allied troops. Livy quotes one source saying the Romans added only 10,000 men to their usual army.

The Carthaginian army may have numbered between 40,000 and 50,000, a figure to be treated with caution, as are all those for the Carthaginian side. Its infantry is estimated at 8,000 Libyans, 5,500 Gaetulians, 16,000 Gauls (8,000 of them left in camp on the day) and 8,000 from Hispania. The cavalry was 4,000 Numidian, 2,000 Iberian, 4,000 Gallic and 450 Libyan-Phoenician, with 1,000 to 2,000 Balearic slingers and 6,000 javelin men. The troops were united by their personal tie to Hannibal.

The Romans drew up in the usual order, infantry in the centre and cavalry on the wings, but deeper than usual to break through Hannibal's centre as they had done at the Trebia. The centre was commanded by Geminus Servilius, Varro had the left and Paullus the right. Hannibal placed his Iberians, Celtiberians and Gauls in the middle, alternating them, with himself and his brother Mago, and the African infantry on the wings. Hasdrubal led the Hispanic and Gallic cavalry on the left by the Aufidus, which protected that flank, and Hanno the Numidians on the right.
sections.course:
The armies had stayed in their camps for two days. On 1 August Hannibal offered battle but Paullus refused, and Hannibal's cavalry then harassed the Romans' water-bearers. Paullus opposed fighting on open ground, where Hannibal held the cavalry advantage, but thought withdrawal unwise. On the morning of the battle the Carthaginians had manoeuvred so that the Romans faced east, with the low sun and dust blown by the wind in their eyes. Appian and Livy say Hannibal sent 500 to 600 men to feign desertion and attack the camp from within, though this is disputed.

Hannibal advanced the centre of his line in a crescent curving towards the Romans. The battle began with a fierce cavalry fight on the wings. The Hispanic and Gallic horse won on the Roman right, and Hasdrubal led them round to the other side to attack the allied cavalry still fighting the Numidians, which broke. As the Roman heavy infantry attacked, Hannibal stood in the weak centre and held it in a controlled retreat, so that the crescent buckled inwards. The Romans, pressing forward, were packed so closely that they had little room for their weapons, and had ignored the African troops on the projecting ends.

The Carthaginian cavalry drove off the Roman horse and attacked the Roman rear. Hannibal ordered the African infantry to turn inwards on the Roman flanks, and the Romans were enclosed in a pocket with no way out. Polybius says that as the outer ranks were cut down the survivors huddled together and were killed where they stood. Livy describes wounded men overpowered by the enemy as they rose from among the dead.
sections.aftermath:
A few Romans escaped. Livy and Polybius agree that Varro got away to Venusia with 70 horsemen. Polybius says perhaps 3,000 infantry and 300 allied horsemen escaped. Livy names 600 men under Publius Sempronius Tuditanus who fought out of the smaller camp, and 4,000 infantry and 200 horsemen from the larger camp who reached Canusium, and says Varro reported assembling 10,000 survivors. Only about 15,000 Romans are said to have survived, most from the garrisons of the camps.

Rome was in panic. The authorities consulted the Sibylline Books, sent Quintus Fabius Pictor to the oracle at Delphi, and buried people alive as a sacrifice. They lowered the draft age and enlisted criminals, debtors and slaves to raise two new legions. Capua, Tarentum, Arpi, Salapia and other southern cities went over to Hannibal. Sicily's Greek cities rose in revolt, Philip V of Macedon pledged support, and Hieronymus of Syracuse made an alliance the next year.

Hannibal's offer to ransom survivors was rejected, and his delegation under Carthalo was refused a hearing on moderate terms. The Senate declared full mobilisation, prohibited the word peace and limited mourning to 30 days. In the story told, the Numidian commander Maharbal urged Hannibal to march on Rome and said that Hannibal knew how to win a victory but not how to use it. Hans Delbrück argued that Hannibal's army, after its losses, could not assault the city; Field Marshal Montgomery believed Maharbal was right. Rome fought 14 more years until Zama.
sections.sources:
There are three main accounts of the battle, none contemporary. The nearest is Polybius, who wrote about 50 years after it. Livy wrote under Augustus and Appian later still. Polybius presents the battle as the lowest point of Roman fortunes, perhaps to stress the later recovery; some say his casualty figures are exaggerated, 'more symbolic than factual'. Livy presents the Senate in heroic terms and puts the blame on the low-born Varro, clearing the soldiers he idealises. Appian's account is unrelated to Livy's and Polybius's, and scholars tend to discount it.

Plutarch gives details, without a connected narrative, in his lives of Fabius and Aemilius Paulus. The date is uncertain, as the pre-Julian Roman calendar did not match the Julian; Macrobius gives 2 August, and Derow identified the Julian date as 1 July. The casualty figures differ widely: Polybius has 70,000 dead and 10,000 captured; Livy 45,500 foot and 2,700 horse dead; Appian and Plutarch 50,000, and Quintilian 60,000. Cantalupi proposed 10,500 to 16,000, and Samuels and Clodfelter also doubt the larger figures.

Who commanded on the day is also in question. The traditional account puts Varro in command and gives him the blame, but Martin Samuels doubts it, because the Senate's warm reception of Varro contrasted with its treatment of other defeated commanders. Gregory Daly notes the Roman right was the place of command, and that Hannibal at Zama claimed to have fought Paullus, so it is impossible to be sure. Some historians call Polybius's account of the crescent fanciful and see a natural bending of the line.
sections.legacy:
Cannae is one of the worst defeats in Roman history. Adrian Goldsworthy compares its death toll to the first day of the Somme in 1916. It led to reforms: the Roman infantry, which had fought in a mass resembling a Greek phalanx, was gradually articulated into small tactical bodies, as at Ilipa and Zama, leading in time to the cohort under Gaius Marius. Unified command came to be seen as necessary, and Scipio Africanus was made general-in-chief in Africa. The battle also exposed the limits of a citizen militia, and the army gradually became a professional force.

The battle became a model. It is called the archetypal battle of annihilation and the first successful pincer movement recorded in detail in the Western world. Dwight D. Eisenhower wrote that every ground commander seeks a battle of annihilation and tries to repeat the example of Cannae. Frederick the Great and Helmuth von Moltke tried to create their own Cannae, and Hans Delbrück's study influenced Alfred von Schlieffen, whose plan was inspired by Hannibal's double envelopment. In 1991 Norman Schwarzkopf named Cannae as an inspiration for coalition operations in the Gulf War.

Some writers question the lesson. Robert O'Connell argues Hannibal's only chance of winning the war was to march on Rome. Others infer from Hannibal's conduct, and from the fact that he first attacked Rome only in 211 BCE, that his aim was to wear the Romans down to a moderate peace by stripping them of allies.

summary: At Cannae on 2 August 216 BCE Hannibal's army surrounded a larger Roman and allied force under the consuls Paullus and Varro and killed most of it, though the Roman dead are put at anything from about 10,000 to 70,000. Rome refused terms and went on to win the war at Zama.
notes: Number to check: the lead says 'approximately 86,000'; Polybius's own total for eight legions is not given in the article; my forces section lists the article's component figures only.
The article says four people buried alive in its lead and 'twice burying people alive at the Forum Boarium' in the aftermath; I wrote 'buried people alive'.
The date: the article gives 2 August (Macrobius) and Derow's 1 July; I gave both. The ev date uses 2 August.

Hannibal's Carthaginian losses (Livy about 8,000; Polybius 5,700) are not in my text because of length; they should be added if a section can be trimmed. Likewise the ransom of the prisoners, Mago's gold rings and Scipio's oath were left out.
Left out for gore and length: Hanson's claim of about 600 killed a minute, Livy's pits and suffocated men, Sabin's verdict on Appian, and Eutropius's figures.
Montgomery's view is given from the article; O'Connell's quotation is paraphrased as 'only chance'.
Left out: Gisgo anecdote, equipment of each side, the Cannae model's long Schlieffen quotation, Dodge's and Durant's praise (praise words).
